subject: barnstormerBiplane
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: barnstormer biplane.
Style: whimsical.
reasoning:
I'm designing a whimsical Stearman-style barnstormer biplane module, roughly 8m long with a 9m wingspan, featuring a chunky round fuselage, oversized propeller, striped wings, and bright cartoonish paint details.

I'm also planning the structural details—wheels, thin strut and wire supports, and a cute pilot figure with goggles and a scarf peeking from the cockpit—keeping everything grounded on the floor plane with wheels touching down and nothing floating above the model. I'm reviewing the builder SDK's available helpers and import paths, favoring the toon kit for its cartoonish cel-shaded look to match the whimsical style.

Now I'm sketching the actual dimensions for a chunkier, whimsical take on a Stearman-style biplane—roughly 5.6 meters nose-to-tail, fuselage centered around 1.25m height with a tapering radius—and starting to place the wheels underneath.

I'm working out the landing gear geometry, with wheels at about 0.36m radius set 1.8m apart in V-strut legs, plus a small tail skid, then moving into the biplane wing layout: lower wing near the fuselage bottom, upper wing about 1.15m above it, spanning roughly 8.4m total with a 1.35m chord.

Defining wing extrusion axes...

I'm sketching the wing outline as a chamfered rectangle in chord-span coordinates, with leading and trailing edges tapering near the tips to avoid sharp corners.

Now I'm thinking through extrusion settings — a moderate thickness with a slight bevel and some corner smoothing to round the tips a bit. I'm also considering adding aileron slabs along the trailing edge as separate colored pieces.

For the wing paint, I'm planning candy-stripe coloring along the span, alternating cream and red bands based on position, and weighing whether to apply toon-style cel shading across the whole plane for a cohesive whimsical look.

I'm tracing through how `cel` handles a nested Paint as its `lit` input — the outer `at(p, n, s)` sets `current` to the surface coordinate, so when the shading function resolves the inner stripe paint without explicit `s`, it correctly falls back to that shared `current` value, letting the two layers compose properly.

Given the complexity of threading `s` through nested paints, I'm weighing whether to skip the toon kit and write my own simpler paint functions instead, but the kit's shading helpers (`cel`, `INK`, `shadowOf`) are documented and give nicer results, so I'll stick with them — using `cel` for the main fills and `INK` for linework. Now I'm sketching the actual plane design: a candy-colored biplane in red and cream with yellow stripes, a big round nose, and painted eyes on the nose for a whimsical face.

I'm planning the eyes using the `animeEye` decal, plus a propeller with a spinner, and a pilot with goggles and a leather helmet whose scarf sweeps back behind the plane like a trailing ribbon. I want the pilot to feel like a small but clear part of the barnstormer theme, kept modest in detail.

For the geometry, I'm working out the fuselage as a swept shape along a path from nose to tail with a varying radius function, considering how to define the radius profile so the nose rounds off nicely before tapering toward the tail.

I'm also weighing whether a sweep (round, whimsical) or a loft with width/height stations (boxier, chubbier, more toylike) better captures a squashed cartoon body, and leaning toward lofting stations from nose to cockpit to tail for a rounder, toy-plane proportions.

I still need to work out how loft's bone parameter should reference a joint, and then plan the skeleton structure starting with a root joint even though this vehicle doesn't strictly need creature-style rigging.

For the skeleton itself, I'll keep it simple: a root "frame" joint, a "prop" joint at the nose for propeller rotation, a "head" joint for the pilot, and possibly aileron joints for the wings. Roles aren't strictly required, so I'll skip assigning them unless it clarifies intent.

I'm figuring out where to attach wheels and other parts to joints, using simple position-only joint definitions that inherit the parent's orientation by default.

Confirming parts can take a bone reference alongside an explicit position, so I'll attach each part to its root joint directly.

I'm defining a small helper to create body parts bound to a given bone, then sketching a whimsical color palette with cream, candy red, and sky blue tones for the body.

Now I'm fleshing out the full color scheme—tomato red with cream panels for the body, striped wings, yellow accents, a wooden propeller with a brass hub, dark wheels with cream hubcaps, and wood-toned struts. I'm also designing the pilot with warm skin tones, brass goggles with glowing blue lenses, and an orange-red scarf with yellow stripes, considering applying a cel-shading effect to give everything a toon-like look.

I'm working through the paint and part budgeting—keeping painted areas efficient within a shared texture sheet, capping flat colors at 64, and targeting roughly 150-220 parts across a sizable module. I'm now planning the fuselage as a lofted shape with a red body, cream cowling band, and yellow side stripe, built along a path using station-based coordinates.

Writing shading helper functions...

Still working out fuselage colors...

I also need to handle the cockpit opening, since sweeps can't create a true cutout. I'm thinking of placing a dark rim or coaming on top of the body instead—maybe a flat cylinder or ring geometry sitting at the cockpit location to give the impression of a recessed well where the pilot sits.

Now I'm sketching out the fuselage loft stations from nose to tail, noting approximate z-positions, center heights, widths, and heights at each station to shape the curved body profile, and figuring out where the wings and cockpit opening should align along that length.

Adding tail station points, then thinking about lower wing placement—it needs to sit beneath the fuselage without intersecting it, so I'm positioning it lower than the fuselage bottom, similar to a Stearman-style biplane layout.

I'm settling on lower wing positioned around y=0.92 with thickness 0.12, letting it pass through and attach to the fuselage bottom so the overlap reads naturally in the biplane silhouette, similar to how a Stearman's lower wing meets the fuselage near ground level.

With the full-height lofting, the body peaks around 1.89 at its widest, so I'm placing the upper wing at y=2.2 with cabane struts bridging the gap from the fuselage top up to the wing's underside. I'm also checking the wheel clearance — centered at y=0.36 with radius 0.36 puts its top at 0.72, leaving a reasonable gap below the lower wing at 0.86, and now working out how the gear legs connect back to the fuselage.

Writing wheel geometry...

Now placing the wheels at the axle positions on the frame bone, and adding a connecting axle rod across the body. Then I'm starting on the lower wing, planning its chord and span outline centered at the right z-position.

For the wing extrusion I'm positioning the origin at [0, 0.92, 0.2] with the chord running along z and the thickness along Y, keeping it symmetric. I'm settling on a biplane layout with equal spans around 8.4 for both lower and upper wings.

Now I'm sketching the wing outline as a rectangle with rounded corners, placing leading and trailing edge points at the span tips and relying on smoothing to round the tips into a soft rectangular shape.

Now I'm thinking about wing paint patterns—chordwise candy stripes across the span, alternating cream and red bands roughly every 0.7m for a whimsical racing-stripe look, though I'm weighing that against a simpler option like a red band near the root versus cream elsewhere.

I'll go with yellow tip caps beyond ±3.4m span for extra flair, and now I'm planning aileron geometry—small rectangular slabs near the outboard trailing edge of each wing, built as separate extrudes with hinge joints so they can articulate independently.

For the interplane struts, I'm working out positions connecting the lower wing top to the upper wing bottom, likely using capsule or rod primitives with a small radius placed symmetrically at a few span locations per side to approximate a biplane strut arrangement.

Still writing strut and bracing rods...

Let me simplify to two bracing bays per side, placing struts near x=1.5 and 3.3, with diagonal wires crossing each bay rather than trying to wire the full span—skipping the fuselage-crossing wires since the fuselage sits between them.

Now for the nose, I'm shaping the engine cowling, spinner, and propeller hub using a lathe profile that defines the spinner's curved cone shape from base to tip.

I need a prop joint for the spinner and blades so they can spin independently — oriented with its bone axis along Z (forward) rather than the default Y, so rotation animation happens about the correct axis.

For the propeller geometry, I'm sketching two blades as thin boxes lying in the XY plane positioned at the nose, with options for either simple boxes or a tapered extruded blade shape for a more realistic look.

This actually gives a single two-bladed propeller shape spanning the hub, extruded with a slight taper, which is a nice simplification. I'm placing the hub pivot at its center and orienting the extrusion axes so the blade thickness runs along Z while the blade plane spans X and Y.

For the blade finish, I want to paint red tips against the natural wood color, checking how far each point is from the hub center along the span. The spinner cone covers the hub via a lathe profile, and everything attaches to a propeller joint for rotation. Now I'm thinking through exhaust stack details—small spikes arranged around the engine cowling.

Rather than modeling the exhausts as separate attached geometry, I'm considering placing them directly on the fuselage surface using a surface-hit placement system: wrapping the loft/sweep mesh with a surface wrapper, then positioning details by azimuth and elevation angles around a chosen center point, figuring out which angle corresponds to which side of the model.

I'm getting playful with the idea of putting a cartoon face on the plane's nose cowling—big googly eyes placed on the flanks near the front, built as custom SVG decals applied to the surface, giving the whole thing a whimsical character.

I'm checking whether the propeller disc, which sits further forward at the nose, would overlap or hide a mouth decal placed below it — since the prop spans wider than the body but sits slightly ahead in z, it shouldn't block the face.

I'll restrict eye placement to around ±30 degrees azimuth to keep them clear of the blades, and double-check the scale: prop diameter near 2.2m lines up reasonably with a real Stearman's ~2.6m prop.

Now I'm working out the pilot's head position relative to the cockpit, sizing the skin-toned head sphere and starting to shape a leather helmet ring around it using a lathe profile.

Positioning goggles on the head...

I'm untangling the local-vs-world axis convention: local +X corresponds to the model's right side, which is world -X, while world +X maps to the model's left. So when looping over s=1/-1 for symmetric placement, s=1 should correspond to the right side using the word-based keys like `right:` rather than raw signed coordinates, to avoid flipping errors.

For the pilot figure I'm keeping it simple: a head sphere, two cylinder goggles positioned in front using word-based offsets (forward/up/right), a lathe-based leather cap, and a swept ribbon for the scarf. I'm working out how to orient the goggles to face forward using the frame's `dir()` method versus explicit world-space direction vectors, since the local-to-world mapping isn't straightforward when the head isn't itself rotated.

Since the head joint stays rigid, I decide it's simplest to just define everything in model-space coordinates attached to the head bone rather than fighting with local direction helpers, and I start setting constants like the head center position and sphere radius, working out where the cockpit body top and head center should sit relative to each other.

I'm figuring out the neck needs a capsule to bridge the gap between head and body, then sketching a scarf ring geometry around the neck using a closed catmull curve.

Adjusting torus rotation to lie flat...

Now I'm sketching the scarf as a ribbon sweep trailing backward from the neck toward the tail, plotting curve points that drift upward and outward as they stream behind the fuselage.

Defining the sweep radius function with flat end caps, then moving to goggles: forward-facing cylindrical lenses positioned around the eyes with a brass rim detail.

Adjusting cap dimensions...

I'm skipping ear flaps and thinking about adding a smile decal to the head using an SVG texture positioned at the front-lower face, though I need to check whether the scarf at the neck would occlude it.

Now I'm positioning a cockpit rim ring around the pilot's hidden torso, working out the cylinder dimensions and placement so it sits tangent to the body's tapered profile at that station.

The neck stays hidden inside the body until it becomes visible around 1.85. I'll skip adding cockpit instruments to keep things simple and whimsical instead. Now I'm working out the tail fin geometry, planning a side-profile outline extruded for the vertical stabilizer positioned behind the body.

Still working out fin geometry coordinates...

Good, thickness runs along -X with a small bevel, and the fin outline is placed at its base point with span along z and height along y, centered on the drawing. I'm thinking the fin should be red with a yellow stripe detail, then moving on to plan the horizontal stabilizer's chord and span placement near the tail.

Now I'm working out the stabilizer's extrusion axes so thickness runs along Y, sketching its rectangular outline with the right chord width at the tail position. For the tail skid, I'm sizing a small capsule rod running from the body near the tail down to just above the ground, checking that its bottom point stays close to zero like the wheels so everything sits properly grounded.

With the wheels confirmed resting exactly at y=0 given their radius, I'm now adding decorative touches: a yellow pinstripe running along the fuselage sides, cream-yellow paint for the nose cowling, and a lower cream panel on the body, working out the coordinate conditions to paint each region correctly.

Defining the color palette and stripe logic...

Working out the wing paint pattern — alternating red/cream chordwise stripes on top, cream fading to blue near the tips underneath.

For the ailerons, I'm planning yellow slabs on the trailing edge outboard of the upper wing, slightly thicker than the wing itself so they read as distinct, positioned to stay coplanar with the wing's top surface.

Defining aileron outline coordinates...

I'm figuring out whether to explicitly set the bone for the aileron joint versus letting it inherit from the at position, and deciding the extra part is worth adding. Then I move on to the wing struts, planning to use rod connectors between endpoints with a specified radius and optional styling.

For joint hierarchy, I'm thinking the whole vehicle can hang off a single root frame joint rather than needing a full skeleton like a creature would, so I'm placing the root at the origin and assigning parts to it explicitly where needed.

Defining child joints for prop, head, wheels (with axle orientation set so rotation happens around the correct axis), ailerons, and the scarf as a non-chain sweep attached to the head bone...

I'm also checking joint naming rules and deciding roles: skipping "leg" for wheels since it doesn't fit, but assigning "fan" to prop, "head" to head, and "hinge" to ailerons.

For decals, I'm figuring out how to place eyes on the nose cowling surface using the loft result treated as a sweep, positioning them around a center point with azimuth and elevation offsets.

Since the googly SVG is symmetrical, no mirroring is needed. For the eye design, I'll go with a white ellipse with a dark outline, an iris with a highlight, placed near the cowl at the right position. I'll skip adding a mouth on the fuselage since it would be hidden by the prop, maybe giving the pilot a small smile instead, and I'm considering a barnstormer-style insignia too.

Now I'm thinking through adding a roundel decal — a circular emblem placed on the fuselage sides, sized appropriately with the decal system's automatic surface projection. I'm also considering a whimsical trailing banner behind the tail, like something a barnstormer pilot would pull, maybe with playful text on it.

I'm reconsidering the banner idea, deciding it falls outside the model's actual bounds and isn't called for in the brief, so I'll skip it along with any smoke trail effects. The scarf covers the "flying accessory" need well enough on its own, and I'm also thinking about adding stripes to the spinner, choosing bold yellow for the struts with dark thin wires, and settling on dark tires with contrasting hubs for the wheels.

Working out wheel hub colors...

For the landing gear, I'm sketching V-shaped diagonal struts connecting the fuselage bottom to the axles, plus a static axle rod running between the wheel hubs that stays fixed while the wheels themselves rotate independently on their own joints. For the propeller, I'm setting up a lathed spinner hub with extruded blades attached to a separate rotating bone.

I'm confirming that parts attached to a bone use model-space positions at rest, so the propeller geometry stays rigid and rotates correctly around the hub's origin point at the nose. Now I'm working out the spinner's lathe profile dimensions so it tapers smoothly into the nose cone's loft without a visible seam.

Checking positioning: the propeller disc should sit just in front of the nose, which ends at 2.25, so placing blades at 2.3 works, with the spinner spanning 2.2 to 2.58 covering the hub where the blades emerge.

Now I'm shaping the blade outline itself, defining the two-bladed prop as a symmetric polygon tapering from a wide hub section near the center out to narrow tips at y=±1.12.

I'm also setting the blade thickness to taper slightly from root to tip, and planning the paint function so the blade reads as wood with red-painted tips near the ends, applying a cel-shaded look to the wood coloring.

Checking that the prop blade geometry doesn't need a spin animation for the rest pose, then moving to verify the wing and fuselage proportions: the lower wing's chord position relative to the fuselage nose and cowling, and making sure the lower wing's bottom clearance sits above the wheel height.

I'm deciding wing spans (lower slightly wider than upper for the biplane silhouette) and placing interplane struts and wires at specific chord and x positions, defining their rod and wire geometry with radius and color parameters, and working out the x-coordinates for the interplane strut locations on each side.

Now I'm figuring out where the diagonal bracing wires go between bays, deciding which strut positions to connect and skipping the central fuselage area, while working out whether the outboard bay needs its own diagonal pairing.

That gives 8 diagonal rods total across both bays and sides, which seems like a reasonable part count. For wing tips, I'll just add stripes via paint rather than extra geometry.

I'm thinking about adding small yellow sphere "bulbs" at the wingtips for a whimsical touch, placed near the outer edges of the upper wing.

For the fuselage roundels, I'm designing a layered circular decal using SVG—cream outer ring with a dark stroke, red middle circle, and blue center—then figuring out where on the fuselage sides to place them using the hull's positioning system.

For the wing roundels, I'll cast a ray downward from above the upper wing surface to find the correct attachment point and orientation for the decal.

I'll size the roundel decal proportionally and place it on the wing top, skip the lower wing roundel and pilot helmet detail for simplicity, and keep the eyes/cowling detail on the nose as planned. Now moving on to the painting step.

For the pilot's skin, I'm placing a sphere for the head using the skin material, then working out where to position a smile decal on its front surface by finding the nearest point facing outward from the head.

Next I'm figuring out goggle lens placement over the eyes, above the smile — calculating the sphere's surface coordinates at the appropriate x offset so the cylindrical lenses sit flush against the head's curve, just below where the helmet covers the top.

Adding the strap torus around the head, orienting it so the ring lies flat around the head at goggle height rather than facing forward.

Next I'm adding a scarf torus around the neck and sizing the neck capsule geometry to fit the pilot's head and torso joints properly.

Checking the scarf's trailing path though — it looks like it would pass right through the tail fin geometry around z -1.56 to -2.44, so I need to route the ribbon higher or reposition it to avoid that collision.

Coloring the scarf with alternating yellow and red stripes along its length, with flat caps on the sweep. Now I'm adding a cockpit rim torus around y 1.86, sized to fit within the body's cross-section width.

I'm running into sizing mismatches between the torus ring and the body's narrowing profile at different z positions, so I'm picking a torus radius around 0.36-0.38 with a thin tube that roughly matches the body width at the cockpit location rather than perfectly contouring it.

For the cockpit interior, I'm adding a small flat-colored cylinder in a dark brown shade sitting at the body's top to suggest a sunken well, keeping it simple without extra cel-shading detail.

I'm counting up textures needed: eye, roundel, and smile so far, with room to add a fin number or fuselage label like "SODA POP" to round out the decal set toward the 5-12 texture target.

Now I'm deciding on a playful fuselage decal text—something like "BARNSTORMER" or "SKY CANDY"—and positioning it so it doesn't collide with the yellow pinstripe or the roundel placement around the fuselage circumference.

I'm working out the decal direction convention: `[1,0,0]` faces outward on the left flank so the text reads correctly from that side, while `[-1,0,0]` does the same for the right flank without needing a mirror flag. Since the hull is symmetric, I'll duplicate the text and roundel decals on both sides using opposite dir vectors.

Now I'm sizing and positioning the fuselage text—roughly 1.3m wide by 0.3m tall, centered around z=0.7—and checking it against the wing geometry to make sure the wing's chord at y≈0.9 doesn't overlap the text band at y≈1.36, which it doesn't since they're in different z ranges.

I notice the yellow pinstripe conflicts with the text center, so I'm shifting the pinstripe down to y=1.2 and recentering the text at y=1.5 with its 0.3 height spanning 1.35–1.65. I'm also sketching the body paint logic: yellow cowling above z=1.45, cream for the belly below y=0.92, yellow for the side stripe, and red elsewhere, then moving on to work out the tail coloring.

For the fin and stabilizer I'm settling on red with a yellow top band for the fin, cream for the horizontal stabilizer, and yellow ailerons. For the undercarriage I'm choosing dark struts for the landing gear legs and yellow for the interplane struts, then detailing the wheels — dark tires, a yellow hub cylinder, and a small red cap on the outer face, with the tires rotating along the axle joint.

Now I'm positioning the wheels at the axle joints, orienting the wheel cylinders so their axis aligns horizontally, and adding a tail skid as a rounded dark rod running from the fuselage down to just above the ground so it doesn't clip through. I'm also sketching out a pair of small exhaust stack pipes on the sides of the cowling near the bottom.

I'm deciding to skip the windshield since biplanes don't typically need one, and I'm working out how to apply surface decals like eyes onto the sweep-based cowling hull, calculating where a ray at a given angle from the center would hit the outer surface to place them correctly.

Writing SVG eye graphic...

Scaling to a 128px raster, the stroke width works out to about 11px, matching the decal size proportions and the 2:1 aspect ratio of the viewBox.

For the roundel, I'm designing a "SKY CANDY" text SVG with serif bold lettering, a dark fill, and a thick cream outline using paint-order stroke so the text pops against the sky background, sized for a 512px raster with a decal around 1.3 units.

That covers the four textures I need -- EYE, ROUNDEL, SMILE, and SKYTEXT -- with decals treated as textured parts that show only front faces, so I'm set on that front.

I'm also considering reusing the ROUNDEL texture as a star emblem on the fin, placed on both sides for visual unity, and working out the ray-casting math to find the correct surface target on the thin fin plane.

Continuing to interpolate the trailing edge z-coordinate at that height, landing around -1.95 to -0.42 depending on the edge, to pin down proper decal placement bounds.

I'm setting up the roundel ray origins for the fin, wing top, and fuselage sides, reusing the ROUNDEL geometry and adding a null-hit guard. For the upper wing roundel, I'm working out the right x-coordinate given the alternating stripe bands on the wing surface.

Now I'm checking which bone the upper wing part belongs to and confirming the joint creation order starts with the root before children like the propeller hub. I'm figuring out the right imports, specifically whether `svg` is exported from the main SDK module.

Finalizing the import list with `createBuilder`, `paint`, `rng`, `svg`, `catmull`, `polyline`, and `bezier`, plus the toon kit import for `cel` and `INK`. I'm also deciding I don't need `rng` since I'm skipping rivets and random tufts, and starting to call `createBuilder` with the model name.

Now I'm drafting the exported metadata object and the default build function, setting up color constants like a red cel shade and cream cel shade with explicit shadow tones, and noting flat dark hex colors are fine for whimsical toon style. I'm starting to set up the root frame joint at the origin, though its position doesn't matter much since body parts are offset separately.

Setting root joint position and hierarchy...

Still defining fuselage stations...

Still writing paint function...

I'm defaulting to RED for the rest of the hull, then thinking about whether to wrap this in a cel shader — being careful that nesting cel inside cel could cause the lit/shadow logic to compound incorrectly since each layer picks its own lit/shadow string based on the same light direction.

The fix is to keep the inner paint returning plain color strings rather than nested Paints, and apply a single cel wrapper at the top level so shadow resolution only happens once instead of doubling up.

Defining the material color constants now...

Defining color constants...

Finishing the wing outline coordinates, I'm checking that the extrude direction maps correctly to the model's forward axis. Applying a small smoothing radius rounds the corners slightly, turning the rectangular wing shape into something with softly rounded tips rather than sharp edges.

Setting up the lower wing...

Adding stripe patterns across the span and setting up aileron outlines for the upper wing, mirroring the shape by side using a sign multiplier on the v-coordinate.

Checking wingtip bulb placement and stripe coloring logic, then starting to build the interplane struts with a loop over strut positions and heights...

Defining shared paint constants...

I'm recalculating the cabane strut positions, checking that x=0.5 falls outside the body's elliptical cross-section at the top and adjusting to x=±0.3 so the struts actually meet the body surface correctly.

Now I'm working out the landing gear geometry, placing rod connections at the body's bottom edge and running them down to the wheel axle positions with appropriate radii.

Adding tire, hub cap, and center details...

I'm adjusting the tail skid rod endpoint so it lines up with the tapered body loft and sits flush at the bottom, then moving on to defining the propeller hub joint and starting its extrusion.

Checking the blade extrusion — thickness runs along the Z axis correctly, tapering linearly from 0.05 at the bottom of the outline to 0.02 at the top, with a toon shader distinguishing wood color from red tips based on surface normal.

Now I'm setting up the hub spinner as a lathe shape centered near the body, revolving around the Z axis. The profile starts at the axis and sweeps outward to form a rounded cap, closing back to the axis so it forms a solid — I'm bumping segments up to 14 for a bit more smoothness, then adding a striped toon paint pattern based on angular position.

For the eyes on the cowling, I'm computing a surface from the hull and using an angular lookup around the body center to find the outer hit point where the eye decal should sit, roughly on the upper front side of the cowling.

I'm checking whether the spinning prop blades would visually block the eyes, but since the blades stay centered near x≈0 while the eyes sit further out at x≈0.45, they should remain clear even as the prop rotates.

Now I'm placing the side roundels on the fuselage, calculating hit points based on body width at that z-position and setting decal size and orientation for both sides.

For the sky text decal, I'm working out where it hits the fuselage near the pinstripe, checking that the text band at y 1.38 sits comfortably above the stripe at 1.2 so they don't visually clash.

The roundel at z -0.5 is far enough from the text's z range to avoid overlap too. For the side decals, I'm making sure the `at: hit` setup auto-aligns the decal's direction to the surface normal, so the left flank text faces outward correctly, and I'm about to work out the mirrored setup for the right side where the normal points the opposite way.

I'm now adding the cockpit disk, checking its placement and radius against the fuselage body's width at that z-position to make sure it sits flush within the rounded top without poking through the edges.
